questions.explanation: For X = Y<sup>2</sup>/Z the percentage uncertainties add, with the power counted: %X = 2 × %Y + %Z. The percentage uncertainty in Y is twice that in Z, so %X = 2 × 2%Z + %Z = 5%Z, D. Many candidates chose C: they handled the square on Y correctly (4) but left out the uncertainty in Z. Many chose B: they either dropped the power of 2 on Y (2 + 1 = 3) or missed that %Y is twice %Z. Write each term out, with its power, before you add.

Most candidates found the resultant by vector addition. One way is to resolve the 8.0 N force along and across the 10 N force: 8.0 cos 60° = 4.0 N along and 8.0 sin 60° = 6.9 N across. Along the 10 N line the total is 14 N, so the resultant is √(14<sup>2</sup> + 6.9<sup>2</sup>) = 16 N, B. Some stopped at the 14 N horizontal total, which is A. A few mixed sine and cosine, which gives about 17 N, C. A few simply added the magnitudes, 10 + 8.0 = 18 N, D.

Most candidates correctly identified the collision as inelastic: the objects stick together, so momentum is conserved and kinetic energy is not, which is A. Many chose B, confusing the conservation of energy with the conservation of kinetic energy. Total energy is always conserved, but some of the kinetic energy has been transferred to other forms such as thermal energy, so the kinetic energy has changed. Others took the collision for an elastic one.

Few candidates chose D, and both A and B were more popular. Before the explosion the momentum is 2mv. Afterwards one half of mass m is stationary, so the other half of mass m must carry 2mv: it moves at 2v. Its kinetic energy is ½ × m × (2v)<sup>2</sup> = 2mv<sup>2</sup>, D. A, ½mv<sup>2</sup>, is what you get by assuming the moving part still travels at v. B came from candidates who found 2v but cancelled it against the ½ without squaring it. The speed is squared in kinetic energy: square it first.

Most candidates recognised that the upthrust is greatest on the object that displaces the most water, so they chose B. Upthrust equals the weight of the fluid displaced. B is fully submerged, so it displaces 2V. D has volume 2V as well, but it is floating, so only part of it is under the water and it displaces less. Many chose D, perhaps reasoning that B must feel an upthrust smaller than its weight while D's upthrust equals its weight, and assuming the two larger objects weigh the same. Weights are not given. The question is about displaced volume.

Very few candidates solved this. Look at the pressure at the level where the oil meets the water in the left arm. The oil above that point must give the same pressure as the water column above that level in the right arm: 850 × 30.0 = 1000 × h, so h = 25.5 cm of water. The oil surface is 30.0 cm above the join, and the water surface in the right arm is 25.5 cm above it, so x = 30.0 − 25.5 = 4.5 cm: A. The different arm areas do not matter, because pressure depends on the height of the column, not its width. Stopping at 25.5 cm gives D.

Use conservation of energy. From X to Z the kinetic energy rises from 5.2 J to 9.6 J, a gain of 4.4 J. The weight is 2.0 N, so X is 4.4 / 2.0 = 2.2 m above Z. Y is 4.0 m above Z, so Y is 4.0 − 2.2 = 1.8 m above X: A. C was the most popular wrong answer: it is the height of X above Z, a good intermediate result, but it is not what the question asks. Some candidates found it and did not use it to get the final height.

Only a minority combined the equation for the change in kinetic energy with the work done. The net work Fs equals the change in kinetic energy, ½mv<sup>2</sup> − ½mu<sup>2</sup>, so 2Fs = mv<sup>2</sup> − mu<sup>2</sup>: B. D was the most popular wrong answer: candidates correctly substituted F/m for a but handled its sign wrongly, because the speed rises, so v<sup>2</sup> = u<sup>2</sup> + 2(F/m)s. A was also popular: it leaves out the ½ in the kinetic energy.

This needed two conversions: energy per unit volume to a power, then total power to wasted power. The fuel gives 1.5 × 10<sup>4</sup> × 34 × 10<sup>3</sup> J per hour, which divided by 3600 s is 142 kW. That is the total input power. The wasted power is what is left after the useful 40 kW: 142 − 40 = 102 kW, A. Many candidates stopped at the input power, 142 kW (B). Some added the useful output to the input, 142 + 40 = 182 kW (C). Ask what the question is asking for before you stop calculating.

Many candidates correctly found the ratio. The graph is a straight line through the origin, so the work is the area under it. From 0 to 10 mm it is ½ × 0.010 × 4.0 = 0.020 J. From 10 to 20 mm it is ½ × (4.0 + 8.0) × 0.010 = 0.060 J. The ratio is 1 : 3, C. Some candidates seemed to treat the force as constant and used W = Fd, which gives the same work for the same extra distance, so A (chosen by many). The force of a spring rises with extension, so the work done is the area under the graph, not force times distance.

Many candidates correctly selected A, showing they understood the definition of the elastic limit: beyond it the deformation is plastic. Many also chose D, confusing the limit of proportionality with the elastic limit. The two are different. Up to the limit of proportionality the extension is proportional to the force. The elastic limit can come a little later, so you cannot say the extension is proportional to the force all the way up to it. Learn both terms and what separates them.

Most candidates chose A or B, so they know the central fringe of this experiment is white. Slightly more chose A than B, which shows they understood that shorter wavelengths are diffracted through smaller angles. Violet is deviated least and red most, so on each side of the white central maximum the violet end of the spectrum is nearest the centre and the red end furthest from it: A. B has the colours the wrong way round. A few chose C, which shows uncertainty about what this experiment produces.

Candidates needed to work out from the 17 nodes that there are 16 half-wavelengths, or 8 complete wavelengths, between X and Y: λ = 0.48 / 8 = 0.06 m. Then f = c / λ = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> / 0.06 = 5.0 × 10<sup>9</sup> Hz, B. The wrong routes each give a printed option. Dividing 0.48 by 7.5 (confusing the nodes between X and Y with the total) gives 4.7 × 10<sup>9</sup> Hz, A. Dividing by 15, the number of nodes between X and Y, gives 9.4 × 10<sup>9</sup> Hz, C. Dividing by 16, the number of half-wavelengths, gives 1.0 × 10<sup>10</sup> Hz, D. Nodes are half a wavelength apart: count the gaps, then halve.

Many candidates combined I = Q/t with I = Anvq to get the average displacement of the free electrons: the displacement is Q / Anq. The area is π(d/2)<sup>2</sup> = π × (2.1 × 10<sup>−4</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 1.4 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, so the displacement is 0.15 / (1.4 × 10<sup>−7</sup> × 8.5 × 10<sup>28</sup> × 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup>) = 8.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m: C. B was a popular distractor: it comes from using the diameter as the radius, which gives an area four times too big and a displacement of 2.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m. The diameter is given, so halve it first.

A few candidates deduced that a fall in the thermistor's temperature raises its resistance, so it takes a larger share of the battery's p.d. and the voltmeter reading increases. To bring the reading back, the thermistor's share has to fall again, which means the variable resistor must take a bigger share: its resistance must be increased: D. Many candidates chose incorrect answers across all the distractors. Two quantities change here, so work the sentence through in two steps: what the thermistor does first, then what the variable resistor must do to undo it.

The circuit symbol for an oscilloscope was not widely known. The most commonly chosen wrong answer was the galvanometer. Candidates are expected to recognise all the circuit symbols listed in the syllabus. The symbol shown, a circle containing a trace, is the oscilloscope: D.

Many candidates confused neutron number with nucleon number and chose A. An α-particle carries away 2 protons and 2 neutrons: its nucleon number is 4, but the neutron number N falls by only 2, and the proton number Z falls by 2. X is at Z = 94, N = 144, so the nucleus moves to Z = 92, N = 142: arrow C. Arrow A drops N by 4, which is the nucleon number. Nuclear physics has many similar-sounding terms, so check which of N, Z and A the axes show.
